Every spring the library in my neighborhood puts a wooden box beside the return slot. Its label says TAKE A SEED, LEAVE A STORY. Inside are paper envelopes filled with basil, beans, sunflowers, and occasionally something mysterious. Last year I picked an envelope marked simply “surprise” and carried it home.

I planted its contents in a chipped blue pot on my windowsill. For weeks nothing happened. I watered the soil, rotated the pot, and apologized to it for the weak afternoon light. Then one morning a small green hook lifted itself out of the dirt. I felt absurdly proud already.

The plant grew quickly, winding around a pencil I had pushed into the pot for support. Its leaves were broad and slightly fuzzy. When a yellow flower appeared, I sent a photograph to my aunt, who knows gardens better than I know my own passwords. “Cucumber,” she wrote back immediately.

By midsummer, the vine had claimed half the window. Its first cucumber was crooked, thumb-sized, and delicious. I sliced it over rice with salt and vinegar, then saved its seeds on a saucer. Watching them dry, I understood why the library asked for stories rather than just another packet back.

A seed is a small wager that the future will offer enough light. It helps to have someone waiting beside the window, even if that someone is only learning how to grow things. This spring, I returned an envelope labeled “cucumber,” with a note inside: Be patient. It starts slowly.
